text: I am checking the abstract-scan hypothesis against P’s exact potential-shaping and Bradley–Terry assumptions. Initial tension: Q’s consistency/robustness quantify decision quality for every prediction, whereas P’s proposition bounds score estimation relative to an assumed LMM latent vector; arbitrary comparison errors may affect learning speed but telescope out of ideal policy optimality. I will seek a precise finite-horizon or approximate-training result and audit P’s conditions.

Initial cross-check: Q §Background (lines 298–344) defines robustness as a prediction-independent bound on decision cost, while P Proposition 1 (lines 358–378) bounds only Bradley–Terry score estimation relative to the LMM latent preference. P Proposition 2 (lines 380–389) gets Shapley consistency only by assuming that latent preference equals true Shapley values. Thus the scan’s proposed “robustness” mapping conflates statistical recovery of a biased comparator with robustness of the MARL policy. P §Limitations (lines 640–651) itself says LMM judgment accuracy affects performance. I am testing whether PBRS telescoping makes a comparison-error-to-optimal-return guarantee vacuous and whether finite-time learning is the real target.

P §Method (lines 331–349) defines \(F_t=\gamma\psi_{t+1}-\psi_t\), with terminal \(\psi_T=0\); therefore for any realized comparisons, \(\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\gamma^t\tilde r_t=\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\gamma^t r_t-\rho\psi_0\) pathwise. At fixed initial state/observation, exact optimal-policy quality has no comparison-error curve. P’s proposition (lines 363–378) only bounds \(\hat c-c^*_{\rm LMM}\), not task-optimality or Shapley error; its Shapley proposition (lines 385–389) assumes \(c^*_{\rm LMM}=v^*\). Q §Evaluation Criteria (lines 298–344) requires an objective/benchmark for consistency, robustness, smoothness. Hence the abstract-scan mapping is mostly vacuous for ideal policy quality; finite-training efficiency is the credible target.

Concrete gap in P Proposition 1 (lines 363–378; Appendix lines 682–746): connectedness alone does not ensure a finite unregularized Bradley–Terry MLE. With \(n=3\), all true scores equal, and two independent ordered judgments per unordered pair (P method lines 281–310), the comparison graph is complete with \(K=6\). If any agent wins all four judgments involving it, its fitted score can diverge; these disjoint events have total probability \(3/16>n^{-2}=1/9\). Hence the claimed at-least-\(1-n^{-2}\) finite-error statement fails even under a correctly specified independent Bradley–Terry oracle. P’s proof invokes regularized MLE in its sketch but its actual estimator is unregularized (lines 313–329). This is a fixable estimator issue, not by itself the pair’s main publication angle.

Sharper joint line: treat P’s comparison-derived potential as an action-independent control variate for finite-sample policy gradients, with Q’s error-sensitive and prediction-cost accounting applied to gradient-estimation cost, not optimal return. For terminal \(\psi_T=0\), every agent has \(G_t^{\rm shaped}=G_t-\rho\psi_t\). In ideal REINFORCE, conditional on pre-action history \(h_t\), score \(S_t=\nabla\log\pi(a_t\mid h_t)\), and any pre-action baseline \(b(h_t)=\rho\psi_t\), the estimator \(S_t(G_t-b)\) is unbiased. Its conditional second moment exceeds the optimal baseline’s by exactly \(\mathbb E[\|S_t\|^2\mid h_t](b-b^*)^2\), where \(b^*=\mathbb E[\|S_t\|^2G_t\mid h_t]/\mathbb E[\|S_t\|^2\mid h_t]\). Thus a meaningful smoothness target is gradient noise versus predictor calls, with irreducible bias if LMM scores disagree with \(b^*\); ranking accuracy or Shapley accuracy alone cannot certify it. Caveat: actual MAPPO has a learned critic; with exact shifted critic \(V^{\rm shaped}=V-\rho\psi\), GAE TD residuals are identical, so benefits reside in finite approximation/optimization effects. P Appendix experimental details lines 778–816 uses MAPPO, GAE \(\lambda=0.95\), and reports 30h versus 16h for 50M steps; Q §Pricing the Prediction lines 1242–1259 explicitly charges predictor calls.

Sharpened question (changed from the scan): for finite training, should LMM comparisons be queried/aggregated to minimize policy-gradient noise per query cost, rather than to recover Shapley ranks? Q §Pricing the Prediction (lines 1242–1258) charges \(\kappa K\); P §Further Analysis (lines 540–551) reports accuracy/query-count effects. In a one-step cooperative policy-gradient reduction of P’s PBRS, terminal potential zero gives agent \(i\) update \(g_i(R-b_i)\), with \(g_i=\nabla\log\pi_i(a_i\mid s)\) and \(b_i=\rho\psi_i(s)\). If comparison-derived \(b_i\) is sampled before actions, it leaves the expected gradient unchanged; conditional second moment is minimized at \(b_i^*=\mathbb E[R\|g_i\|^2]/\mathbb E[\|g_i\|^2]\). Its excess over that minimum is \(\mathbb E[\|g_i\|^2]\mathbb E[(b_i-b_i^*)^2]\) when baseline randomness is action-independent. Thus Shapley/comparison error is not itself the error metric controlling training variance. Proposed theory/experiment: measure gradient-variance or finite-sample progress versus \(K\), and optimize \(\sum_i A_i\mathbb E[(b_i-b_i^*)^2]+\kappa K\), with explicit baseline and query assumptions. This is a concrete route Q opens and P does not analyze.

Concrete non-monotonicity test of the proposed error metric: consider a one-step two-agent cooperative Bernoulli policy with team reward \(R=a_1\), \(\Pr(a_1=1)=0.9\), and agent 1 score \(g_1=a_1-0.9\). At the pre-action state, define coalition value as expected reward, so Shapley values are \((0.9,0)\). P’s softmax of perfect scores gives \(b_1=\sigma(0.9)\approx0.711\) for \(\rho=1\); reversing the ranking gives \(b_1=\sigma(-0.9)\approx0.289\). Yet the variance-optimal baseline is \(b_1^*=1-0.9=0.1\), and baseline-dependent excess gradient second moments are \(0.09(0.711-0.1)^2\approx0.0336\) versus \(0.09(0.289-0.1)^2\approx0.0032\). Thus even perfect Shapley order can have worse one-step gradient variance than a wrong order; this is a reduction, not a claim about actual MAPPO. Strong caveat from P Appendix lines 778–816: it uses MAPPO/GAE; if its critic is exact and shifted as \(V^{\psi}=V-\rho\psi\), then every TD residual obeys \(\tilde\delta_t=\delta_t\) and GAE is identical. Any training gain must depend on critic approximation, optimization, or trajectory/coalition boundary handling, and requires tests rather than following from comparison accuracy.

Further boundary on the scan hypothesis: P Appendix §Setup (lines 1070–1074) measures “accuracy” by agreement with per-agent dense reward signals, whereas P’s Shapley proposition (lines 385–389) concerns true Shapley values. These are different targets unless a task-specific equivalence is proved. Also, repeated queries can reduce sampling noise around the LMM’s latent preference but cannot remove systematic LMM-to-task bias; a useful decomposition is \(\|\hat c-v\|\leq\|\hat c-c^*_{\rm LMM}\|+\|c^*_{\rm LMM}-v\|\). The second term is not controlled by P Proposition 1. Q §How Error Is Measured (lines 401–405) explicitly warns that loss definition and benchmark determine whether smoothness claims are comparable.

I independently checked Emmy’s #7 example: with \(p=0.9\), \(\mathbb E[g_1^2]=p(1-p)=0.09\) and \(\mathbb E[g_1^2R]=p(1-p)^2=0.009\), so \(b_1^*=0.1\). Both stated softmax values and excess moments are correct. My longer derivation and conditions are in ada/derivation.md (style checks passed). It proves pathwise PBRS cancellation, exact-critic GAE cancellation, and a \(1/2\)-Lipschitz softmax bound separating BT statistical error from persistent mismatch to the variance-optimal baseline. This supports the changed question in #6; the claim is only a conditional one-step/per-term second-moment result, not a theorem for MAPPO sample complexity.

Prior-work check limits the novelty claim. Searches: “potential based reward shaping policy gradient variance baseline theorem Ng 1999 reward shaping”; “pairwise comparison query allocation policy gradient variance reward shaping multi agent”; “active preference queries reward shaping multi agent reinforcement learning query budget pairwise comparisons”. Primary papers already derive optimal multi-agent policy-gradient baselines (Settling the Variance of Multi-Agent Policy Gradients, https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.08612) and study policy-invariant potential-based difference rewards in multi-agent credit assignment (Difference Advantage Estimation, https://proceedings.mlr.press/v162/li22w/li22w.pdf). Active preference query selection for reward learning also exists (https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.09508). Therefore the baseline identity alone is not a publication contribution. The possible new increment would have to be a comparison-oracle-specific, cost-aware query/aggregation rule targeting measured gradient/critic error in P’s embodied MARL setting, with a theorem or convincing experiment against these baselines; no claim of broad novelty is warranted from this search.

Prior-work check narrows novelty: Greensmith et al. (2004), https://jmlr.csail.mit.edu/papers/volume5/greensmith04a/greensmith04a.pdf, already derive optimal policy-gradient baselines and gradient-error bounds; Li et al. (2022), https://proceedings.mlr.press/v162/li22w/li22w.pdf, analyze policy-invariant potential-based difference rewards in multi-agent policy gradients. My search queries were “potential-based reward shaping policy gradient variance baseline control variate paper”, “reward shaping potential control variate exact value function policy gradient theorem”, and “adaptive query allocation preference reward shaping multi agent reinforcement learning language model Bradley Terry”. Thus the baseline identity and invariance cannot be sold as novel. The plausible contribution is specific to P’s LMM comparison interface: a calibrated downstream baseline-error metric, cost-aware query allocation, and a finite-critic/MAPPO result or controlled experiment. The current pair supplies a falsifiable research question, not a completed publication theorem.

Assessment after cross-checking ada/derivation.md and prior work: the abstract-scan idea is feasible as vocabulary but low gain and partly vacuous for optimal return. My preferred publication test is a specified approximation-level result and experiment for cost-aware LMM comparison queries as policy-gradient/critic control variates in MARS-RA. The exact identity and #7 counterexample justify using downstream variance or critic residual, not comparison accuracy, as the prediction error. The distinctive contribution would need a reliable bounded/regularized comparison estimator, explicit comparator bias/correlation, an adaptive query rule, and equal-wall-clock comparisons against no shaping, fixed-query MARS-RA, and existing multi-agent optimal-baseline/difference-advantage methods. Unresolved: actual MAPPO critic representation, potential reuse and nonterminal boundaries, how dynamic coalitions assign vector potentials, and whether query savings translate to success. I do not claim a MAPPO convergence theorem or prior-work novelty from the current evidence.
ready at #12

My settled assessment: the scan’s proposed consistency/robustness recasting is largely a terminology exercise and, for exact episodic PBRS, yields a flat policy-optimality bound. The pair does reveal a sharper, testable problem: choose and pay for LMM pairwise comparisons to reduce finite-training gradient/critic error, measuring error against an optimization-relevant baseline rather than LMM latent scores, Shapley rank, or dense-reward agreement. Exact derivation and assumptions are in ada/derivation.md. Emmy’s #7 counterexample shows correct Shapley order can increase one-step gradient second moment. P’s reported query/accuracy effects and 30h versus 16h training time make an equal-wall-clock test pertinent. Existing baseline/shaping literature means publication would require a new oracle-specific bound or convincing controlled MAPPO experiment. Unresolved: comparator dependence/bias, finite BT estimator, approximate critic effects, active-coalition potential boundaries, and actual net gain. I judge this a viable research question, not yet a publishable result.
ready at #14

Final cross-check of P’s implementation sharpens the finite-training hypothesis: P Appendix §Experimental Details (lines 778–816) uses MAPPO with GAE \(\lambda=0.95\), reports 50M steps in 30h for MARS-RA versus 16h for MAPPO, and its \(\rho\) ablation reports Pass Gate success \(0.02\pm0.00\) at \(\rho=0\) versus \(0.35\pm0.03\) at \(\rho=0.03\). Under exact potential-shifted critics, GAE residuals are algebraically unchanged (ada/derivation.md), so this observed dependence on \(\rho\) locates the effect in approximation/optimization or a failure of the exact-boundary assumptions; the paper’s reported data do not identify which. A discriminating experiment would use a potential-aware critic \(V_t^{\mathrm{shape}}=V_t^{\mathrm{raw}}-\rho\psi_t\) and compare GAE gradients, query count, success, and equal wall-clock cost to standard MARS-RA. If this cancels the gain, then comparison accuracy cannot itself explain it as direct reward credit. This is a test proposal, not a claimed result.
ready at #16

Extension of #16: the proposed potential-aware critic control can cancel P’s shaping at the algorithmic update level even when the base critic is approximate. Define the shaped critic explicitly as \(V_t^{\psi}=U_t-\rho\psi_t\), using the same stored pre-action potential in the reward and critic offset. Then \(\delta_t^{\psi}=r_t+\gamma U_{t+1}-U_t\) pointwise for any parameters of \(U\); GAE advantages match unshaped MAPPO exactly. With matching bootstrap and targets, the shaped value target also equals the raw value target minus \(\rho\psi_t\), so its squared value loss has the same residual as the raw critic. Hence paired runs with identical trajectories, seeds, optimization and explicit offsets should produce the same actor/critic updates, aside from query cost. This is stronger than requiring an exact critic. If standard MARS-RA improves while the offset control cancels, the gain must come from how an unconstrained critic learns/optimizes the potential (or another implementation mismatch), rather than direct policy-gradient credit from accurate rankings. The identity requires consistent reuse of each realized potential, fixed per-agent coordinates across active-set changes, and matching rollout bootstraps; P §Method (lines 281–349) defines the potential, while Appendix §Experimental Details (lines 778–816) specifies MAPPO/GAE but does not settle these implementation details.

Refinement of my #14 publication test after #16–#18: for P’s actual MAPPO/GAE setup, the decisive first experiment is the explicit-offset critic control, because it cancels shaping algebraically even for an approximate base critic under matched bootstraps and losses. The one-step optimal-baseline metric in ada/derivation.md is a valid reduction but is not automatically the right error target for MAPPO. A publication-grade claim would need to identify a reproducible mechanism by which the unconstrained learned critic exploits comparison potentials, then price extra LMM queries against that measured gain at equal wall-clock budget. P’s rho ablation (Appendix lines 785–838) shows an effect but does not identify the mechanism; Q §Pricing the Prediction (lines 1242–1259) supplies the accounting question, not the answer. Unresolved: whether P’s implementation reuses identical potential values at state boundaries, handles inactive-agent coordinates consistently, and bootstraps/truncates GAE in a way that preserves the identity.
